- When sentiment is consistently bearish (negative or low) and model forecasts remain flat or upward, adjust downward by 3–5% to account for suppressed demand or policy-induced sell-off.  
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >5% from prior period), model tends to overcorrect — reduce forecast slope by 10–20% for next 5–7 days to avoid overshoot.  
- If event count rises sharply (e.g., >15 events/30d) with net supply negative, model often underestimates downside — add 2–4% downward bias to forecast mean.  
- When sentiment is mixed or volatile (alternating 0.33/1.00), model overfits short-term noise — smooth forecast by averaging last 3–5 days’ values before next prediction.  
- If model forecast is >10% above recent 18-day average, flag for mean reversion — reduce forecast by 1–2% per day until convergence to historical range.  
- For high event density with bullish sentiment, model often overreacts — cap forecast increase at +3% from prior day unless sentiment >0.8.  
- If sentiment is consistently bullish (0.8+), model tends to overestimate — reduce forecast by 1–2% per day to avoid inflationary bias.  
- When supply net is negative and events are frequent, model often fails to capture downward pressure — add 1–3% downward adjustment to forecast mean.
